title: HAWK-I infrared image of the spectacular barred spiral galaxy NGC 1365
caption: The barred spiral galaxy NGC 1365 in infrared light, imaged by the Very Large Telescope
celestial: NGC 1365 · constellation Fornax · about 60 million light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: Official ESO press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: This infrared image shows NGC 1365, a barred spiral galaxy, photographed with the powerful HAWK-I infrared camera on ESO's Very Large Telescope at Paranal Observatory in Chile.

A barred spiral is a spiral galaxy with a straight band of stars running across its centre, with the spiral arms trailing from the ends of the bar. NGC 1365 is a member of the Fornax galaxy cluster, roughly 60 million light-years from Earth.

Infrared light passes through much of the dust that blocks visible light, so infrared observations reveal the stars and structure of a galaxy in a different way than an ordinary photograph. HAWK-I took images through four filters, called Y, J, H and K, each sensitive to a different slice of infrared light. Exposures lasted 4, 4, 7 and 12 minutes in turn, and the four were then combined.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (6.50 x 6.45 arcminutes) and distance (60 million light years), the frame spans roughly 113,000 × 113,000 light-years. Its light set out about 60 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This image comes from the HAWK-I infrared camera on ESO's Very Large Telescope, combining Y, J, H and K infrared filters. The source does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Infrared light is invisible to the human eye, so the colours here stand in for wavelengths we cannot see.
